t.2.10.1: Having given orders for the consecration of Rāghava, the self-controlled great king entered the inner apartments to tell the pleasant news to his beloved, who was worthy of good tidings.
t.2.10.2: The lord of the earth, as if scorched by grief, saw her there, fallen upon the ground and lying in a manner unbefitting her.
t.2.10.3: That old man, himself without sin, saw lying on the ground his young wife, dearer to him even than his life, whose intent was sinful.
t.2.10.4: As a great elephant in the forest might tenderly caress a female elephant pierced in the woods by a hunter's poisoned arrow, so he lovingly stroked her.
t.2.10.5: Stroking her with both his hands, his mind gripped by alarm, the love-struck king spoke these words to the lotus-petal-eyed woman.
t.2.10.6: I do not understand this anger that has taken hold of you. O queen, by what have you been afflicted, or by whom have you been slighted?
t.2.10.7: That you lie here in the dust, O lovely one, brings me grief; why do you lie upon the ground when my heart is well disposed toward you, like one whose mind is struck by a spirit, you who torment my heart?
t.2.10.8: I have skilled physicians, well contented in every way; they will make you well again. Tell me your ailment, O lovely lady.
t.2.10.9: For whom should a kindness be done for your sake, or by whom has something displeasing been done to you? Who is to receive favour today, or who a very great displeasure?
t.2.10.10: Who that does not deserve death shall be put to death, or who that deserves death shall be set free? Which poor man shall become rich, or which wealthy man shall become penniless?
t.2.10.11: I myself and all who are mine are obedient to your will; I cannot bring myself to thwart any wish of yours.
t.2.10.12: Tell me what you desire in your heart, even if it must be paid for with my own life; as far as the wheel turns, so far does the earth belong to me.
t.2.10.13: Thus addressed, she, now reassured and wishing to speak that disagreeable thing, set about tormenting her husband further.
t.2.10.14: I have not been wronged by anyone, my lord, nor have I been dishonored. But I have a certain wish, and I want it fulfilled by you.
t.2.10.15: Make a solemn promise, if you wish to do it; then I shall declare what has been desired by me.
t.2.10.17: O proud one, do you not know that, apart from Rāma, that tiger among men, there is no man dearer to me than you?
t.2.10.18: Good lady, having searched even this heart of mine, draw it out. Having considered this, Kaikeyī, tell me what you think is right.
t.2.10.19: Seeing the power you hold within yourself, you ought not to doubt me. I will do what pleases you; I swear to you even by my good deeds.
t.2.10.20: Delighted by that speech, she declared her intention, terrible in the extreme, like Antaka, Death, come upon him.
t.2.10.21: As you swear in due order and grant me a boon, let the thirty-three gods, led by Indra, hear it.
t.2.10.22: The moon and the sun, the sky, the planets, night and day, the directions, the world, and the earth together with its Gandharvas and Rākṣasas.
t.2.10.23: May the beings that roam by night, the household deities dwelling in the houses, and whatever other beings there are, take note of what you have said.
t.2.10.24: This man, true to his promise, of great splendor, knowing dharma and fully composed, is granting me a boon; let the deities hear my words.
t.2.10.25: Having thus secured the great archer and charged him with his promise, the queen then spoke these words to the boon-giver, who was deluded by desire.
t.2.10.26: The two boons that you granted me then, O god, O lord of the earth, those two I shall name this very day; hear my words.
t.2.10.27: The preparations for the consecration of Rāghava have been made; with this very consecration let my Bharata be consecrated.
t.2.10.28: For nine and five years let Rāma dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest as an ascetic, wearing bark garments, a deerskin and matted locks.
t.2.10.29: Let Bharata enjoy this very day the office of heir apparent, free of all rivals; and this very day may I see Rāghava departing into the forest.
t.2.10.30: Then, having heard Kaikeyī's cruel words, the great king was pained and utterly distraught, like a deer that has caught sight of a tigress.
t.2.10.31: Seated upon the bare ground, sighing long and deeply, the lord of men, filled with indignation, uttered the words "Alas! Shame!" and then, his mind struck down by grief, fell once more into a swoon.
t.2.10.32: After a long while the king, deeply grieved, regained consciousness, and in his anger he spoke to Kaikeyī as if burning her with his eyes.
t.2.10.33: O cruel woman of wicked conduct, destroyer of this family, what wrong has Rāma done to you, O sinful one, or even I?
t.2.10.34: Rāghava always bears himself toward you as he would toward his own mother; for what reason, then, are you now bent upon his ruin?
t.2.10.35: Out of ignorance I brought you, a king's daughter, into my own house for my own destruction, like a she-serpent of deadly venom.
t.2.10.37: I could abandon Kausalyā or Sumitrā, or even my royal fortune, or my own life, but never Rāma, who is so devoted to his father.
t.2.10.36: When the whole world of living beings here sings the praise of Rāma's virtues, on the grounds of what offense shall I abandon my beloved son?
t.2.10.38: Supreme joy arises in me when I behold my eldest son; but when I do not see Rāma, my very consciousness is lost.
t.2.10.39: The world might endure without the sun, or the crops without water, but without Rāma my life would not remain in my body.
t.2.10.40: Enough, then! Let this resolve be abandoned, O you of wicked resolve. See, here I touch your feet with my head; be gracious to me.
t.2.10.41: That lord of the earth, lamenting like one without a protector, his heart seized by that immoderate woman, fell toward both of the queen's outstretched feet without touching them, like a man stricken with illness.
